uncited: What sets this family apart from its siblings is the focus on low-level data placement (bit interleaving, bank skewing, block packing) rather than high-level traversal algorithms or indexing structures; it builds on [Dense grids and memory layout](3-dense-grids-and-memory-layout.md) by defining exactly how the dense grid is laid out in bytes.
All methods in this family map 3D spatial coordinates $(u, v, w)$ to a linear memory address or buffer index to improve spatial locality.
The core mechanism involves decomposing the volume into small, fixed-size blocks (miniblocks, chunks, or tiles) and applying a transformation to the coordinate bits or block indices.
Register-form kernels read every shell of a chunk from groupshared memory: centre, cutoff, $l$, AO count, primitives, and rows of $C$.
Inner loop no longer waits on dependent global loads per shell.
The concept of memory layout optimization for volume rendering originated with the need to overcome the limitations of standard 3D array storage when accessed along arbitrary ray directions.
These methods are widely used in high-performance volume rendering systems, particularly in scientific visualization and medical imaging, where large datasets and real-time performance are critical.
